questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I applied to study abroad particularly for the opportunity to attend UC Berkeley. It is not only one of the best public universities in the US, but also well-known for being progressive both academically and non-academically.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I found the orientation information very easily accessible, and everything one needed to know was clearly communicated via email. So remember to check it!

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: If I'm not wrong, there was an option to be met by a ''mentor'' of sorts at the airport - I did not choose to do this. The orientation for international exchange student - called something along the lines of ''Golden Bear Orientation'' - was not the best. It is required (and expensive!), and while there were many activities offered to get to know other students and transfers, not everyone showed up. The food options that were included in the price were also subpar.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It is not too difficult to find housing in Berkeley, it is just really expensive! I found mine through Facebook (there's several groups for people looking for and offering housing off-campus) and ended up in a lovely, big house shared with seven other girls - both students and non-students. For anyone coming here, I would definitely recommend finding other people in your age to live with, and to not be afraid to share a room. While it is not common to have roommates in Denmark, it is completely normal here and a good learning experience (even if you end up learning that you prefer to have your own room). Having a roommate (or two) can also help temper with the rental price, which is absurdly higher than in Copenhagen for what you get.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: First of all - the quality of housing is not as high as in Scandinavia, and while you might be paying a lot, that doesn't ensure quality. Try having a good relationship with your landlord or rental agency, they are there to make sure you your space is safe and functioning.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You register through CalCentral (Berkeley's own student website), where you receive a ''registration window''. This is essentially a period of time - usually a couple of days - in which you can register for your classes. More than often these classes are first-come-first-served. In some cases, you need a teacher's permission to enroll in their course, so for that you have to email them and ask beforehand. There is an adjustment period a few weeks into the semester, where it is possible to switch out classes if you did not find a right fit.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The enrollment process was well-described on their website, and there was also the opportunity to contact advisors or anyone else in a suitable position for help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I had no problems enrolling in any of my classes, although it did take some time for me to figure out the system with ''reserved seats'' (which are seats in a course reserved for a special group of students - so while there might be 5 seats free in the course it could still be full if you do not fall into that special category).

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember to check requirements, and how many seats are available for your student status. Email any professors for courses where you need their professors beforehand. Also, make a list (with backup-choices too!) of the courses you are planning to take before the registration window opens.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took mostly undergraduate upper-division level courses at Berkeley, since I experienced they fit me best. Within my program, this usually meant that they consisted of smaller groups and were seminar-based, aka filled with discussions. I also took a graduate seminar which was challenging but very fun! As a senior student I also took (and dropped) a freshman class the first semester, since I found it a bit too easy, and the general crowd was very young.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Most of my courses were discussion-based and not lectures. We were all expected to have done the readings before class and everyone is encouraged to speak (indeed, your grade is often dependent on it). There were also weekly presentations by students which were the ground material for student discussions.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 2 semesters

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: For anyone in the literature-field, I would recommend taking one of the senior seminars in the Comparative Literature-department. You are also allowed to take one graduate course per semester, which can be an interesting (and very rewarding) experience. However, not all professors admit undergraduates into their graduate courses. It is also nice to embrace the ability to ''shop around'' for courses, and try something new in a field outside of one's own. I took both a practical art class and a language course here, which was a lot of fun.

questions.answer: None that weren't expected, it was just all very expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I knew housing was expensive, but wasn't prepared for the equally high living expenses, like food.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were many non-academic opportunities to get involved in, although I did not really make use of them.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are so many, and really everything imaginably possible. Most clubs and societies set up tables on the road before Sather Gate, so one can usually find something interesting there.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Although I myself did not participate, I have had friends engaged in both choirs, dance clubs and sports. It is easy to join these things and they are also looking for new members. If one is more culturally inclined, there is also the BAMPFA student committee, which is connected to the local art gallery.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Get around the Bay if you can! Make friends that have a car, or rent one (or use public transport). Both Oakland and San Francisco are great to explore by foot, but it is a bit trickier if you want to get across the bridge into Marin County. However, you are greatly rewarded with incredible nature and beaches. Enjoy the landscape of California and go on hikes, try surfing or other water-activities.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy, since Berkeley in its values is a bit more similar to Denmark than the rest of the US. People are very talkative, and you fall into the ''small talk'' with the cashier or bartender quickly.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: This I found quite difficult, and the ones I met were through my classes. Since everyone has their individual schedules, it can be tricky to catch people before or after classes, so make use of the small breaks (if you get any).

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: People are usually down to chat, but less good at making concrete plans. Try reaching out if you find someone interesting and ask them to hang out with an actual date and time set in mind.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed the easiness with which people communicate with each other, and how open people are.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be open to other people and don't be afraid to make small-talk. 
2. Use the academic opportunities available to you, and try something new both academically and non-academically.
3. Get out and get around! Berkeley is beautiful, but there is so much more to experience and see around the Bay Area and in California (and the US as a whole).

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: It can be a bit unsafe, so don't go out alone at night, especially not if under the influence of alcohol.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting some really special people and getting to learn from some fantastic professors and students. And the weather!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: My greatest challenge was trying to balance academic work with social life, and finding people with whom I share interests on such a big and busy campus.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
